issues.legal_issue: A final determination of title in a land acquisition reference operates as res judicata in a later suit between the parties when title was necessarily and substantially in issue.
material_facts: Rival claimants sought compensation for acquired property on the basis of competing claims to the same share of an estate.
The apportionment dispute required the court to decide which claimant held title to that share.
The title question was contested through the lower courts and finally decided on appeal.
issues.conclusion: The final title determination in the land acquisition proceedings barred the rival claimant from relitigating title in the subsequent possession suit.
issues.legal_principle: Res judicata rests on general principles of jurisprudence, not solely on section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. A decision on title in a compensation reference is binding when title was necessarily and substantially determined. The Court applied Ramachandra Rao v. Ramachandra Rao and Bhagwati v. Ram Kali, and referred to the general principles discussed in Sheoparsan Singh v. Ramnandan Singh, Badar Bee v. Habib Merican Noordin, and Hook v. Administrator-General of Bengal.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference and rival_title_claims and title_necessary_to_apportionment and title_decided_finally and same_parties_or_privies

predicates.land_acquisition_reference: A dispute over compensation for acquired property was referred to a court for determination.
predicates.rival_title_claims: Competing claimants asserted that they held title to the property or share relevant to the compensation.
predicates.title_necessary_to_apportionment: The entitlement to compensation depended on resolving the competing claims to title.
predicates.title_decided_finally: The court finally determined the title question after it was contested.
predicates.same_parties_or_privies: The later dispute over title involved the same parties or persons claiming through them.

issues.definition: When a final decision in a compensation reference necessarily resolves title between the same parties or their privies, that decision bars them from relitigating title.

issues.legal_issue: A difference between compensation money in the earlier proceeding and property in the later suit does not prevent res judicata when both proceedings require determination of the same title.
material_facts: The earlier land acquisition proceeding concerned compensation for acquired property.
The later suit sought possession of property associated with the same disputed share of the estate.
The earlier decision had determined the title on which the compensation claim depended.
issues.conclusion: The difference between the subject matter of the two proceedings did not prevent the earlier title decision from operating as res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: The test is identity of title in the two litigations, not identity of the actual property involved. The Court relied on Bhagwati v. Ram Kali, where a decision concerning compensation for acquired property barred a later claim concerning other property when the same title was at issue.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference and later_property_suit and same_title_issue_decided and title_necessary_to_compensation

predicates.land_acquisition_reference: A court decided a dispute over compensation for acquired property.
predicates.later_property_suit: A later suit concerned possession or title to property beyond the compensation money.
predicates.same_title_issue_decided: The title question in the later suit was the same title question determined in the compensation proceeding.
predicates.title_necessary_to_compensation: The entitlement to compensation depended on deciding that title question.

issues.definition: A difference between compensation and property does not defeat preclusion when the earlier proceeding necessarily decided the same title later disputed.

issues.legal_issue: A decision by a court with jurisdiction to decide the issue in a special proceeding can operate as res judicata even if that court could not try the later ordinary suit.
material_facts: A special judge appointed under land acquisition legislation decided the competing title claims in the compensation proceeding.
The special judge had jurisdiction to determine the title issue necessary to resolve the compensation dispute.
The special judge would not have had jurisdiction to try the later ordinary possession suit.
issues.conclusion: The special judge’s decision could operate as res judicata despite the judge’s lack of jurisdiction to try the later suit.
issues.legal_principle: For res judicata founded on general principles, the former court must have been competent to decide the matter before it; it need not have jurisdiction to try the later suit. The limitation in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure concerning the former court’s competence to try the later suit applies to suits under that section, not to the general principle. The Court relied on Ramachandra Rao v. Ramachandra Rao and Bhagwati v. Ram Kali.

rule.if: special_proceeding and former_court_competent_on_issue and issue_decided_finally and later_suit_raises_same_issue

predicates.special_proceeding: The earlier decision was made in a proceeding exercising a court’s special or exclusive jurisdiction.
predicates.former_court_competent_on_issue: The court had authority to decide the issue that arose in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.issue_decided_finally: The court finally decided that issue.
predicates.later_suit_raises_same_issue: A later ordinary suit raises the issue already decided.

issues.definition: A final decision by a court competent to decide the issue in a special proceeding binds in a later suit raising that issue, even if the former court could not try that suit.

issues.legal_issue: A mortgagee who intervenes in a land acquisition proceeding and defends the mortgagor’s title is bound by the final adverse determination of that title.
material_facts: Mortgagees intervened in the compensation proceedings and claimed compensation under their mortgage interest.
Their claim depended on their mortgagors holding title against the competing claimant.
The mortgagees were represented and defended their mortgagors’ title through the lower courts, and were parties to the final appeal, though they did not appear at its hearing.
The final decision rejected the mortgagors’ title.
issues.conclusion: The mortgagees were bound by the final decision and could not reassert their mortgagors’ title in the later suit.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 9, 10, 18 and 30 of the Land Acquisition Act, an interested mortgagee who intervenes and whose compensation claim is affected by a title dispute may protect the mortgagor’s title. A mortgagee’s interest is tied to the mortgagor’s title; sections 58 and 73 of the Transfer of Property Act recognize the mortgage interest and the mortgagee’s entitlement concerning compensation for acquired mortgaged property. A party that contested the issue in the lower courts is not relieved from the final decision merely because it did not appear at the final appeal hearing.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference and mortgagee_intervened_for_compensation and claim_depended_on_mortgagor_title and mortgagee_defended_title and title_decided_against_mortgagor

predicates.land_acquisition_reference: A dispute over compensation for acquired property was referred to a court.
predicates.mortgagee_intervened_for_compensation: A mortgagee participated in the proceeding and claimed compensation based on its security interest.
predicates.claim_depended_on_mortgagor_title: The mortgagee’s claim depended on the mortgagor holding title against another claimant.
predicates.mortgagee_defended_title: The mortgagee took part in defending the mortgagor’s title in the proceeding.
predicates.title_decided_against_mortgagor: The final decision rejected the title on which the mortgagee’s claim depended.

issues.definition: A mortgagee that intervenes to pursue a claim dependent on the mortgagor’s title and defends that title is bound when the title is finally rejected.

issues.legal_issue: A later possession suit is not barred by the rule requiring execution of an earlier decree when a compromise made that decree unexecutable and the claimant’s later right gave rise to a fresh cause of action.
material_facts: An earlier decree for possession had been affected by a compromise in appeal and the property was partitioned under the compromise.
The compromise was later declared inoperative against the claimant.
The earlier decree had become unexecutable after the compromise, and the claimant sought possession on a later-accruing right.
issues.conclusion: The later suit was not barred by section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure; the claimant could bring a separate suit for possession.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that section 47 did not bar a separate suit where the earlier possession decree became unexecutable because of a compromise that was later held not binding on the claimant, and the claimant had a fresh cause of action for possession. No earlier case was relied on for this ruling.

rule.if: subsequent_possession_suit and earlier_possession_decree and compromise_made_decree_unexecutable and compromise_not_binding_on_claimant and fresh_cause_of_action

predicates.subsequent_possession_suit: A claimant brought a later suit seeking possession of property.
predicates.earlier_possession_decree: A decree for possession had been made in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.compromise_made_decree_unexecutable: A compromise altered the position so that the earlier decree could no longer be executed to obtain the claimed possession.
predicates.compromise_not_binding_on_claimant: The compromise was held not to bind the claimant.
predicates.fresh_cause_of_action: A later-accruing right gave the claimant a new basis to seek possession.

issues.definition: A later possession suit is not barred when an earlier decree became unexecutable through a compromise that does not bind the claimant and a fresh cause of action arose.

issues.legal_issue: A reversioner’s suit for possession is not barred by a predecessor’s failure to sue when the predecessor had no cause of action against persons who were not yet in possession and the reversionary right accrued later.
material_facts: The persons later resisting possession were not in possession during the predecessor’s lifetime.
The predecessor therefore had no cause of action to eject them during that lifetime.
The claimant’s right as the next reversioner arose only upon the death of the intervening holder.
The opposing side had earlier abandoned limitation and adverse-possession pleas, and those pleas had been rejected in the acquisition proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The predecessor’s failure to sue did not bar the claimant’s later suit, and the possession during the intervening holder’s lifetime did not confer title against the claimant.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the asserted limitation premise was incorrect because the predecessor had no cause of action while the opposing claimants were not in possession. The reversioner’s title to seek possession arose only when succession opened. The Court also noted that limitation and adverse-possession pleas had been abandoned earlier and rejected in the land acquisition proceedings.

predicates.reversioner_possession_suit: A claimant sued for possession in the capacity of a person entitled to succeed after an intervening holder.
predicates.defendants_not_in_possession_during_pred: The persons resisting the later suit were not in possession while the predecessor was alive.
predicates.reversionary_right_accrued_later: The claimant’s right to possession arose only after the intervening holder’s death.

issues.definition: A reversioner’s suit is not barred by a predecessor’s inaction when the defendants were not then in possession and the reversionary right accrued later.
